The syntax {auto-animate=TRUE .smaller} ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1,2,3"} # .cell-code} ~ my_component_name( main = ..., model = ... ) ``` ::: - `my_component_name` how you label your component (.e.g, `beta_0`,`myspde`) - `main` input data for the component (e.g., a the name of a column in your data or a spatial object) - `model` The type of model component (e.g., `linear`,`fixed`,`iid`,`rw1`,`rw2`,`ar1`, see `?INLA::inla.list.models()$latent`) ::: :::: ## The syntax pred, family = ... , data = ... , ...) # Fit the model fit <- bru(comps, lik, ...) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **linear predictor** - can be defined within the formula: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lik = bru_obs(formula = response ~ component_1(...) + component_2(...), family, data) ``` ::: - or use a full stop shortcode after the componets have been {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="9,10,11,12,13|16,17"} # Define model components comps <- component_1(...) + component_2(...) + ... # Define the model predictor pred <- linear_function(component_1, component_2, ...) # Build the observation model lik <- bru_obs(formula = pred, family = ... , data = ... , ...) # Fit the model fit <- bru(comps, lik, ...) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Likelihood** Specify the distribution family (see `inla.list.models("likelihood")`) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lik = bru_obs(formula, family = "gaussian", data = df) ``` ::: ::: :::: # Temporal Dependence ## Modelling temporal dependence {.smaller} Data are often observed in time, and time dependence is often expected. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](slides_recap1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: . . . - Observations are correlated in time ## Motivation {auto-animate="true" .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Smoothing of the time effect $$ \begin{aligned} y_t|\eta_t & \sim \text{N}(\mu,\tau_y^{-1})\\ \eta_t & = \mu = \beta_0 + u_t \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} The models we covered: $$ \begin{aligned} 1.\ u_t&\sim \text{RW}1(\tau)\\ 2.\ u_t&\sim \text{RW}2(\tau)\\ 3.\ u_t&\sim \text{AR}1(\tau, \phi)\\ \end{aligned} $$ ::: :::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](slides_recap1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## Gaussian Markov Random Fields (GMRF) {.smaller} ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: A random vector $\mathbf{u} = (u_1, \ldots, u_n)^\top$ is a **Gaussian Markov Random Field (GMRF)** with respect to a graph $G = (V, E)$, with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and precision matrix $\mathbf{Q}$, if its probability density is $$ \pi(\mathbf{u}) = |\mathbf{Q}|^{1/2}(2\pi)^{-n/2} \exp\left\{ -\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{u}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \mathbf{Q} (\mathbf{u}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) \right\}. $$ The precision matrix $\mathbf{Q}$ satisfies the Markov property: $$ Q_{ij} \neq 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \{i,j\} \in E, \qquad i \neq j. $$ Thus, conditional independence between two components $u_i$ and $u_j$, given all the remaining components, is encoded by zeros in the precision matrix: $$ u_i \perp u_j \mid \mathbf{u}_{-(i,j)} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad Q_{ij} = 0. $$ ## Discrete time models {auto-animate="true" .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Random Walks** - *RW1*: Assume independent first-order increments $\Delta u_t = u_t − u_t−1 \sim N(0, \tau^{−1})$ - *RW2* Assume independent second-order increments $\Delta^2 u_t = u_t - u_{i-t} + u_{i-t} \sim N(0, \tau^{−1})$ :::{.fragment} - Intrinsic model $\rightarrow$ sum-to-zero constrain. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp = ~ Intercept(1) + time(year, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE, hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.5, 0.5)))) ``` ::: ::: :::{.incremental} - Small $\tau$ $\rightarrow$ large variation $\rightarrow$ less smooth effect - Large $\tau$ $\rightarrow$ small variation $\rightarrow$ smoother effect - PC-prior: $\text{Prob}(\sigma>U) = \alpha$ $\rightarrow$ penalize models with small precision or large variances (Baseline $\tau=0$). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **AR(1)** - $u_t = \phi u_{t-1} + \epsilon_t; \qquad \phi\in(-1,1), \ \epsilon_t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^{-1})$ :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pc_prior <- list(theta1 = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)), rho = list(prior = "pc.cor0", param = c(0.5, 0.3))) cmp = ~ Intercept(1) + time(year, model = "ar1", hyper = pc_prior) ``` ::: ::: :::{.incremental} - The precision $\tau$ - PC prior $\text{Prob}(\sigma > U) = \alpha$ (Baseline $\tau=0$). - The autocorrelation parameter $\phi\in(0,1)$: - PC prior $\text{Prob}(|\rho| > u) = \alpha$ (Baseline $\phi = 0$ `pc.cor0`) - PC prior $\text{Prob}(\rho > u) = \alpha$ (Baseline $\phi = 1$ `pc.cor1`) ::: ::: :::: ## Continuous time models - Sometimes the data are not collected at discrete time points but over continuous time - One solution (not a bad one usually) is to discretize the time (or covariate) and use RW model (`inla.group()`). - A different solution is to use a continuous smoother based on a continuous Gaussian Random Field (GRF) $\omega(t)$ ## The SPDE {.smaller} We define a (Matérn) GRF as the solution of a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) $$ (\kappa^2-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}\omega(t) = W(t) $$ - $W(t)$ is random noise - $\omega(t)$ is the smooth process we want - $(\kappa^2-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}$ is an operator that "smooths" the white noise. - $\kappa$ and $\alpha$ are parameters :::{.fragment} Approximate the solution (i.e. the GF) by a GMRF defined on a discretized domain or mesh using FEM. $$ \omega(t) = \sum_{i = 1}^T\psi_i(t)w_i $$ ::: :::{.fragment} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} The GF has a Matérn Covariance characterized by - The range $\rho$ - The marginal variance $\sigma^2$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Define PC-priors: - $\text{Prob}(\rho<\rho_0) = p_{\rho}$ - $\text{Prob}(\sigma > \sigma_0) = p_{\sigma}$ ::: :::: ::: ## Fitting a SPDE in 1D 1. Define a 1-dimensional mesh over the domain of interest ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # domain of interest 0-10 locs = seq(-3,13,1) mesh1d = fm_mesh_1d(locs, degree = 1, boundary = "neumann") ``` ::: 2. Define the SPDE model and the prior ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh1d, prior.range = c(10, 0.5), # Prob(range<10) = 0.5 prior.sigma = c(1, 0.5) # Prob(sd>1) = 0.5 ) ``` ::: 3. Use the SPDE model in a component of your model ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp = ~ Intercept(1) + smooth(covariate, model = spde) ``` :::
